meta.description: Jackie Robinson really wrote it. Wikiquote sources the line to his 1972 autobiography I Never Had It Made; it is also carved on his Brooklyn headstone.

source.excerpt: A life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives.
trail: Wikiquote’s cited entry ↗ lists the sentence in its Quotes section with a full citation to I Never Had It Made (1972), “as told to Alfred Duckett,” excerpted in Newsday on 5 November 1972.
The Simple English Wikiquote entry ↗ gives the same book and adds that the line comes from the epilogue.

The book is catalogued as Robinson and Duckett, New York: Putnam, 1972 ↗ — borrow-only at the Internet Archive, so the page itself could not be read directly. That record’s own edition field reads “A Fawcett Crest Book,” a later paperback imprint, so the scan is not claimed here as a first edition.

Independent corroboration that these are treated as his words: the U.S. House entered the sentence into the Congressional Record of 16 April 1997, p. H1580 ↗, and Wikipedia ↗ records it as the inscription, with his signature, on the family headstone at Cypress Hills Cemetery.
source.excerptNote: I Never Had It Made is still in copyright and is not freely readable online, so no fuller passage can be reproduced here. Wikiquote records this exact wording and cites it to the book; the Simple English edition places it in the epilogue.

author.name: Jackie Robinson
author.heading: Who was Jackie Robinson?
author.metaLine: 1919–1972 · First Black player in modern Major League Baseball
author.bio: Jack Roosevelt Robinson broke Major League Baseball’s colour line when he started at first base for the Brooklyn Dodgers on 15 April 1947, and went on to win the inaugural Rookie of the Year Award that season and the National League MVP in 1949. He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1962, his first year of eligibility. After baseball he was a businessman, newspaper columnist and outspoken civil rights advocate; he died of a heart attack on 24 October 1972, aged 53, in the same month his autobiography I Never Had It Made was published — Kirkus gives Putnam’s publication date as 25 October, the day after his death, and Newsday serialised the book that November.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The author is right — this really is Robinson. What circulates badly is everything around the sentence: which book it comes from, whether it comes from a book at all, and the exact words.

items.why: A different Robinson autobiography. Goodreads’ quotes page for that work ↗ lists this line under it — a community submission, not a verified citation. The sourced attribution is to I Never Had It Made.

A public-speaking site titles its post “Jackie Robinson: A life is not important except in its impact on other lives” while the quotation printed in the body of that same post reads “except in the impact it has on other lives” — both on the same page ↗. The body form is the one Wikiquote records; the shortened title form is the one that travels.
The most-shared copy of the line, Goodreads’ quote page ↗, gives no book, no year and no page, and carries the site’s own warning that quotes are added by users and are not verified.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Robinson’s own: Wikiquote’s cited entry ↗ traces it to I Never Had It Made (1972), and his family had it carved on the Cypress Hills headstone alongside his signature.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: Robinson spent his career being measured in firsts — first Black player in the modern major leagues, first Rookie of the Year, first Black National League MVP. The sentence he left behind refuses all of that. It says the scoreboard is the wrong instrument entirely: a life registers only in other lives.

He had reason to think about it. His eldest son, Jackie Jr., was killed in a car crash in June 1971 at twenty-four. Robinson himself, diabetic and nearly blind, made his last public appearance at Game 2 of the 1972 World Series on 15 October, where he used the microphone not to accept applause but to say he would be more pleased when he could look at the third-base coaching box and see a Black manager. He died nine days later. The autobiography carrying this line was published that same month.
context.detailsSummary: How a book’s closing thought became a national shorthand
detailsBody: The quotation travelled first as an epitaph. Tens of thousands lined the route to Cypress Hills Cemetery in Brooklyn, where Robinson was buried beside his son Jackie Jr. and his mother-in-law Zellee Isum; the family headstone carries the sentence above his reproduced signature, which is why so many people meet the line on a stone rather than on a page.

By the fiftieth anniversary of his debut, it had become the standard way to sum him up. On 16 April 1997 a member of the U.S. House read it into the Congressional Record — “In the words of Jackie Robinson ‘a life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives’” — during the tributes marking that anniversary.

The cost of that popularity is sourcing noise. Most quote sites now reproduce the sentence with no citation at all, some with the wording gently rearranged, and at least one filing it under the wrong Robinson book.
context.pull: The sentence he published in his last year is the one carved on his headstone.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Jackie Robinson entry, in its Quotes section (the article has no section titled "Sourced"), attributes with a full citation "A life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives" to I Never Had It Made (1972) by Robinson, as told to Alfred Duckett, excerpted in Newsday, 5 November 1972.
Simple English Wikiquote cites the quote to I Never Had It Made: An Autobiography of Jackie Robinson (1972) by Jackie Robinson and Alfred Duckett, Epilogue.

The Congressional Record, House, 16 April 1997, page H1580, reads: "In the words of Jackie Robinson 'a life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives.'" during tributes on the 50th anniversary of his major-league debut.

Wikipedia records that the Robinson family headstone at Cypress Hills Cemetery bears the quotation "A life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives" inscribed with Robinson's signature; also that he debuted 15 April 1947, was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1962 in his first year of eligibility, made his final public appearance on 15 October 1972 at Game 2 of the World Series, died 24 October 1972 aged 53, and that his son Jackie Jr. died in a car accident on 17 June 1971 at age 24.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of "I never had it made" by Robinson, Jackie, 1919-1972 and Duckett, Alfred, publisher New York, Putnam, 1972, ISBN 0399110100 — borrow-only.
Goodreads' quotes page for the work "Jackie Robinson: My Own Story" lists "A life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives" under that book — the wrong source.
Goodreads' standalone quote page for this line gives no book, year or page, and carries the notice that quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.

This post's title renders the quote as "Jackie Robinson: A life is not important except in its impact on other lives" while the quotation displayed in its body reads "A life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives" — the title variant and the canonical wording on one page, with no source cited.

Kirkus Reviews lists "I Never Had It Made" by Jackie Robinson with Al Duckett, publisher Putnam, with "Pub Date: Oct. 25, 1972" and a review issue of 1 Oct. 1972 — i.e. the stated publication date falls the day after Robinson's death on 24 October 1972.
AZQuotes cites the line to "I Never Had It Made: An Autobiography of Jackie Robinson", book by Jackie Robinson and Alfred Duckett, 1972.
